summary:
Alaska stands within the United States national framework, so the federal document rules bind every traveller arriving in Juneau, Anchorage or anywhere else in the state. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, new passports are issued only as M or F on the supporting documents submitted, and passports already issued with an X remain valid only until expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the Department to proceed with its changed treatment. A visitor's passport can therefore mismatch their presentation and be lawfully refused a matching marker.

Entry screening carries two further national exposures. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25', and that an applicant declaring a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently. At checkpoints, the National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose trans status to TSA officers and other passengers.

Alaska's own record is graded Moderate in Erin In The Morning's national legal-risk assessment of July 2026, grouped with Kentucky and North Carolina: states that have passed one or two laws aimed at transgender adults, enacted multiple laws targeting transgender youth, or are advancing negative laws quickly. That places Alaska above the worst-law and do-not-travel tiers and below the protective groupings, slightly below the national score of 0.36. Idaho was flagged do-not-travel on 13 July 2026, bringing the total of so-designated states to four; Alaska is not among them.

Restriction in Alaska has arrived through appointed regulatory boards rather than the legislature. The Alaska State Medical Board, whose members are appointed by Gov. Mike Dunleavy, voted unanimously on 22 August 2025 to recommend restricting medical care for transgender youth and approved a draft regulation classifying gender-transition care for anyone under 18 as 'unprofessional conduct' subject to disciplinary action. That draft must still be vetted by the Alaska Department of Law and then pass through a 30-day public comment period, so it is not yet in force. No adult-care ban accompanies it.

Facility rules in Alaska are local rather than statewide. The Matanuska-Susitna Borough School District board voted 5-1 on 19 October 2022 to permanently require transgender students to use bathrooms matching their sex at birth or a private option such as the nurse's office, overturning guidelines that had stood for more than seven years; AP described the policy as an apparent first for Alaska. It binds a school district, not adult access to public facilities, and no adult facility ban is recorded for the state. Nine states and one territory do have school and government-building bathroom bans, and in April 2025 a trans student was arrested and handcuffed at the Florida state capitol in what civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Gov. Dunleavy's earlier bid to limit transgender students' access to single-sex facilities failed, while a board he appointed limited transgender girls' participation in girls' sports teams. Twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no facility ban at all, and the Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out state by state which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates, so the document rules a visitor encounters after entry depend on the state involved. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth.

Foreign governments have responded publicly to the federal document and data rules. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States, advisories that followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues.
tangentialFactors:
Alaska's Moderate grading sits in a national spread that runs from protective groupings at one end to four do-not-travel states at the other, with Idaho the latest so designated on 13 July 2026. The 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures driving nationwide trends, and rights groups describe the Kansas statute invalidating non-matching birth certificates and licences as a template other legislatures are following, with further targeting bills pending.

The mechanism of restriction in Alaska differs from the state-level statutory pattern visible elsewhere. Where Kansas legislated and Florida's bathroom law produced an arrest, Alaska's pressure has come through boards appointed by the governor: a failed facility bid, a sports-participation restriction, and a medical-board resolution on youth care. A school district, not the state, moved first on bathrooms.

Comparatively, Alaska has no adult facility ban, unlike the nine states and one territory that do, and no adult-care restriction in the medical-board draft, which reaches only under-18s. Alaska also lacks any protective statute recorded in the July 2026 assessment.

The board's 22 August 2025 vote was unanimous but the regulation is not yet in force.

Transgender girls' participation in girls' sports teams is limited under a rule adopted by a board appointed by Gov. Mike Dunleavy. His earlier attempt to restrict transgender students' access to single-sex facilities did not succeed.

In the Matanuska-Susitna Borough School District, transgender students must use the bathroom matching their sex at birth or a private alternative such as the nurse's office, under a policy adopted 5-1 on 19 October 2022 that replaced guidelines in place for over seven years. outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Alaska Department of Law approved the medical board's draft regulation, and whether the 30-day public comment period has since opened or closed, is unresolved in the sources available here; the draft's current status should be verified before publication.

The board's August 2025 meeting was scheduled to vote on formally opposing 'treatment of gender dysphoria in minors' and on a statement opposing late-term abortion; the outcome of the first of those votes, beyond the reported unanimous recommendation on youth care, is not sourced here.

The scale of the sports-participation restriction adopted by the appointed board, including which sports and age bands it covers, is not detailed in the inventory.

The July 2026 assessment's exact numerical score for Alaska is not given, only that it falls slightly below the national score of 0.36.
